Stereotyping as the reduction of a group to a few simplified, often exaggerated traits, with an attributed definition

claims.claim: Representation analysis examines who appears in media, how often, and in what roles, treating patterns across many texts as the object of study rather than any single character.
A stereotype is a generalized belief about a category of people, an expectation applied to every member of a group; media stereotyping reduces a group to a few simplified, often exaggerated traits.
Stereotypes can be positive as well as negative; a positive stereotype still applies one fixed expectation to every member of a group and remains a reduction.

Symbolic annihilation is a term first used by George Gerbner in 1976 to describe the absence or underrepresentation of groups in media; Gaye Tuchman divided the concept into omission, trivialization, and condemnation.

The Gerbner and Gross formulation that representation in the fictional world signifies social existence while absence means symbolic annihilation frames absence itself as a meaningful object of media analysis.

Cultivation research, founded by George Gerbner with Larry Gross and colleagues, studies consistent patterns of content across television and asks whether long-term exposure relates to viewers' perceptions of social reality.
Media are shaped by the cultural and economic contexts in which they are produced and tend to reproduce dominant, often unexamined norms, while remaining able to reflect cultural change.

A countertype inverts a stereotype's traits into a positive mirror image but remains a reduction defined by the original stereotype, so presence or positivity alone does not constitute complex representation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether media portrayals directly change viewers' attitudes toward the groups portrayed.
positions: Cultivation research, begun by Gerbner and colleagues, argues that consistent exposure to media patterns can relate to viewers' perceptions of social reality.
Critics of strong media-effects claims note that effects are contested, vary by individual, content, and context, and are difficult to demonstrate causally.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes patterns of content and the scholarly question about them; it does not assert direct effects on any individual viewer, and it frames cultivation as research on content patterns over time.

sourceRecords.title: How to Watch a Movie
sourceRecords.provider: University of Arkansas Libraries Pressbooks / Russell Leigh Sharman
sourceRecords.notes: Chapter read directly via curl with a browser user-agent. Supports: cinema as shaped by its historical and cultural context; a cultural feedback loop in which cinema both influences and is influenced by its context; the tendency of an expensive mass medium to reproduce dominant, often unexamined norms; the role of production access in shaping which stories get made; and the book's organization of 'Representation in Cinema' as a recognized dimension of cinema study. Synthesized in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How to Watch a Film
sourceRecords.notes: Two-page MIT OpenCourseWare handout; PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally. Supports film analysis attending to ideology and politics, including sexual or racial difference, class, nation, and generation, and to spectatorship, the question of how a film imagines its viewers. Used to place representation among recognized dimensions of film analysis. Id and URL reused from the sibling narrative topic's evidence packet.

sourceRecords.title: Symbolic annihilation
sourceRecords.notes: Article read directly (HTML fetched and text-extracted). Supports: first use of the term by George Gerbner in 1976 to describe the absence or underrepresentation of groups in media; Gaye Tuchman's (1978) division of the concept into omission, trivialization, and condemnation; and the Gerbner and Gross formulation that representation in the fictional world signifies social existence while absence means symbolic annihilation. The underlying primary source (Gerbner and Gross, 1976, Journal of Communication) is paywalled and was not directly read; the attribution is cited as presented by this reference, which the lesson states.

sourceRecords.title: Stereotype
sourceRecords.notes: Article read directly (HTML fetched and text-extracted). Supports the standard definition of a stereotype as a generalized belief about a category of people, an expectation applied to every member of a group, and the points that stereotypes can be positive, negative, or neutral, are often faulty, and resist new information. Used for the attributed definition and the positive-stereotype point; original wording not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Cultivation theory
sourceRecords.notes: Article read directly (HTML fetched and text-extracted). Supports: cultivation theory founded by George Gerbner with Larry Gross, Michael Morgan, and Nancy Signorielli; message system analysis as the study of patterns of content in television and media; and the theory's proposition that the more time people spend in the television world, the more likely they are to believe social reality aligns with portrayed reality. Used to frame the scholarly question about media patterns and perceptions; the lesson does not assert direct effects on individuals.
